# SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks

Pengbo Shen    Yaqing Wang    Ni Mu    Yao Luan    Runpeng Xie    Senhao
Yang    Lexiang Wang    Hao Hu    Shuang Xu ^(†)^(†)thanks:
Corresponding authors.    Yiqin Yang²²footnotemark: 2    Bo
Xu²²footnotemark: 2

###### Abstract

Evaluating large language models (LLMs) in complex decision-making is
essential for advancing AI’s ability for strategic planning and
real-time adaptation. However, existing benchmarks for tasks like
StarCraft II fail to capture the game’s full complexity, such as its
complete game context, diverse action spaces, and all playable races. To
address this gap, we present SC2Arena, a benchmark that fully supports
all playable races, low-level action spaces, and optimizes text-based
observations to tackle spatial reasoning challenges. Complementing this,
we introduce StarEvolve, a hierarchical framework that integrates
strategic planning with tactical execution, featuring iterative
self-correction and continuous improvement via fine-tuning on
high-quality gameplay data. Its key components include a
Planner-Executor-Verifier structure to break down gameplay, and a
scoring system for selecting high-quality training samples.
Comprehensive analysis using SC2Arena provides valuable insights into
developing generalist agents that were not possible with previous
benchmarks. Experimental results also demonstrate that our proposed
StarEvolve achieves superior performance in strategic planning. Our
code, environment, and algorithms are publicly available.

## 1 Introduction

The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) ([Achiam et al.
2023](#bib.bib1); [Guo et al. 2025](#bib.bib4)) has accelerated research
towards artificial general intelligence ([Mon-Williams et al.
2025](#bib.bib10); [Zheng et al. 2025](#bib.bib29)). A critical
milestone in this pursuit is the development of agents capable of
strategic planning and real-time adaptation in complex environments.
StarCraft II, a renowned real-time strategy game, provides an ideal
testbed with its profound strategic depth, diverse unit types and
interactions, vast decision space, and inherent demands for world
modeling, as illustrated in Fig.
[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks").
These characteristics align closely with the LLMs’ core strengths ([Wei
et al. 2022](#bib.bib23); [Yao et al. 2023](#bib.bib25); [Wang et al.
2023b](#bib.bib21)), making it particularly suitable for LLM evaluation.
Therefore, establishing benchmarks in StarCraft II to assess LLM
performance is critical. However, existing LLM benchmarks in StarCraft
II ([Ma et al. 2024](#bib.bib9); [Li et al. 2024](#bib.bib6)) often fail
to capture the original game’s complexity, lacking support for
full-length game context, complete low-level action spaces,
comprehensive race configuration, and agent-vs-agent mechanisms. This
limits their ability to evaluate the strategic reasoning and
adaptability of LLM agents.

![Refer to caption](2508.10428v1/sc2_illustration_1_v2.png)

![Refer to caption](2508.10428v1/sc2_illustration_2_v2_bg_wide.png)

Figure 1: An illustration of StarCraft II. StarCraft II is a highly
complex and competitive real-time strategy game, where players choose
one of three distinct races (Terran, Zerg, Protoss) to gather resources,
construct buildings, produce units, and defeat enemies. Each race has
unique traits and can produce race-specific buildings and military
units.

To bridge this gap, we propose SC2Arena, a comprehensive StarCraft II
benchmark for evaluating LLMs’ decision-making ability. With a
standardized JSON interface, it supports ① full-length game context, ②
all playable races (Terran, Protoss, Zerg), and ③ complete low-level
actions, preserving the game’s strategic depth. Crucially, SC2Arena
addresses inherent challenges of text-based agents by optimizing
observations: proximity-based unit ordering captures units’ spatial
relationships, and worker aggregation reduces information overload.
Additionally, it enables agent-vs-agent gameplay, facilitating direct
competition and an agent ranking mechanism to better evaluate
performance and strategic adaptability.

Furthermore, we introduce StarEvolve, a closed-loop agent framework that
enables self-correction and self-improvement for strategic
decision-making. It employs a hierarchical architecture: a Planner
generates high-level strategic commands, while an Executor converts them
into precise low-level actions. Both components integrate Verifier
modules that perform iterative self-correction to ensure syntactic
correction and feasibility. Crucially, StarEvolve achieves continuous
self-improvement by collecting gameplay data and performing supervised
fine-tuning (SFT). We design an RL-inspired scoring function to
prioritize high-quality training samples, which quantifies action impact
through discounted value increments across key game-state metrics.
Utilizing these data, we fine-tune the Planner, Executor, and Verifiers
to continuously improve their performance.

In summary, our contributions are twofold: (1) We propose SC2Arena, a
comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LLMs in StarCraft II, supporting
full-length game context, all races, full action spaces, and
agent-vs-agent gameplay. (2) We propose StarEvolve, a closed-loop agent
framework, which integrates strategic planning with tactical execution.
It achieves self-correction with iterative decision refinement, and also
continuous self-improvement via SFT, enabling LLM agents to defeat
challenging opponents.

## 2 Related Work

LLM as autonomous agents. Recent advances in LLMs have empowered
autonomous agents to succeed in diverse domains, including
conversational games ([Xu et al. 2023](#bib.bib24); [Wang et al.
2023c](#bib.bib22)), webpage navigation ([Lai et al. 2024](#bib.bib5)),
and open-world environments ([Wang et al. 2023a](#bib.bib20)).
Concurrently, benchmarks ([Liu et al. 2023](#bib.bib8); [Zhou et al.
2023](#bib.bib30); [Light et al. 2023](#bib.bib7); [Rismanchian et al.
2024](#bib.bib13)) have emerged to evaluate these agents’ planning and
reasoning capabilities. Despite these successes, LLM agents remain
relatively underexplored in real-time adversarial games, which require
integration of long-term strategic planning and precise tactical
execution, under partial observability and time constraints.

AI in StarCraft II. StarCraft II remains a classical AI research
environment ([Ontanón et al. 2013](#bib.bib11)) due to its expansive
action space and real-time decision complexity. Prior work primarily
leveraged reinforcement learning (RL), achieving strong micro-management
performance through multi-agent RL ([Samvelyan et al. 2019](#bib.bib14);
[Rashid et al. 2020](#bib.bib12); [Yu et al. 2022](#bib.bib27)).
Subsequent efforts like ([Vinyals et al. 2019](#bib.bib19)) scaled RL to
full-length game contexts, although this approach required massive
training resources and carefully engineered rewards. In contrast, LLMs
offer complementary strengths to strategic planning by leveraging
inherent world knowledge and reasoning capabilities ([Yildirim and Paul
2024](#bib.bib26); [Yuan et al. 2024](#bib.bib28)). Yet, current
benchmarks for evaluating LLM decision-making in StarCraft II ([Ma
et al. 2024](#bib.bib9); [Li et al. 2024](#bib.bib6)) have limitations,
including the abstraction of low-level tactical execution, a lack of
support for full-length game contexts and full race configurations, and
insufficient agent-vs-agent mechanisms. To bridge these gaps, we propose
SC2Arena, a comprehensive StarCraft II benchmark to evaluate agents
across diverse dimensions. We further propose StarEvolve, a
self-improving agent framework for this benchmark, advancing LLM-driven
decision-making in complex environments.

## 3 Benchmark: SC2Arena

In this section, we propose SC2Arena, a structured text-based benchmark
designed to evaluate LLM agents in StarCraft II, with standardized
observation and action interfaces. SC2Arena supports full-length game
contexts, complete low-level action spaces, all three races and
agent-vs-agent gameplay, thus preserving the original game’s strategic
depth and complexity.

### 3.1 Introduction to SC2Arena

Overview of StarCraft II. StarCraft II is a highly complex and
competitive real-time strategy game, where players control one of three
distinct races (Terran, Zerg, Protoss) to gather resources, construct
buildings, produce units, and command armies to defeat opponents. As
shown in Fig.
[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks"),
the game demands proficiency in macro-management, like resource
management and base-building, micro-level unit control, and strategic
decision-making, all under real-time constraints and partial
information. Its observation space can reach up to 1,200 dimensions,
while the action space can extend to 300 dimensions. Professional
matches typically last 20–30 minutes, with players executing hundreds of
actions per minute. This complexity makes it both a popular AI benchmark
and a globally renowned e-sport.

Each race in StarCraft II offers a distinct playstyle and unique
mechanics, as shown in Fig.
[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks"):
Terrans are a human race with mechanized, repairable units. Their unique
Bio-ball Micro-Tactic involves tightly grouped armies supported by
Medivacs (flying medical transport units). By optimizing unit
positioning and treating injured units, this strategy maximizes
firepower and survivability. Zerg are a swarm-based alien race with
rapidly breeding biological units to overwhelm opponents. Their unique
Creep Spread Mechanism enhances unit speed and vision, enabling
aggressive expansion and superior map control. Protoss are an advanced
alien race with regenerating shielded units. Their unique Warp-in
Deployment mechanic allows armies to instantly arrive at strategic
locations within their Pylon network, enabling precise timing attacks.
Appendix
[A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Introduction to StarCraft II ‣ Appendix A Implementation of SC2Arena ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks")
offers further details.

Improvements over prior benchmarks. As shown in Table
[1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks"),
while prior benchmarks mainly focus on micro-management scenarios
([Samvelyan et al. 2019](#bib.bib14); [Li et al. 2024](#bib.bib6)) or
high-level strategic decision-making ([Ma et al. 2024](#bib.bib9)), our
benchmark, SC2Arena, offers a more comprehensive evaluation platform
covering full-length game contexts that combine strategic planning and
tactical execution. Unlike existing LLM-agent benchmarks ([Ma et al.
2024](#bib.bib9)), SC2Arena supports agent-vs-agent gameplay, enabling
mechanisms such as self-play and agent ranking to advance competitive AI
development. Moreover, compared to [Ma et al. (2024)](#bib.bib9),
SC2Arena supports all three races, enables gameplay on any map, and
offers precise control over the complete low-level action space,
preserving the game’s original complexity and richness.

![Refer to caption](2508.10428v1/agent_illustration.png)

Figure 3: Illustration of StarEvolve. The Planner produces strategic
commands, while the Executor generates executable actions, both
incorporating Verifiers to enable iterative self-correction.
Furthermore, StarEvolve achieves self-improvement by collecting gameplay
trajectories, selecting high-quality or contrastive samples, and
employing supervised fine-tuning.

### 3.2 Benchmark Design

To enable LLM agents to play StarCraft II effectively, game states must
be converted into textual observations, which presents two key
challenges: (1) Spatial reasoning difficulty: Agents struggle to infer
positional relationships between units based solely on text ([Sharma
2023](#bib.bib15)). This hinders agents’ ability to identify attached
and interactable unit structures, such as adjacent Barracks and Tech
Labs, thereby reducing their effectiveness. (2) Information overload:
Raw observations often include excessive low-value data, such as
repetitive worker unit statuses, which overwhelms agents and distracts
them from strategic decision-making ([Adejumo and Johnson
2024](#bib.bib2)).

To address these issues, SC2Arena introduces two key techniques, as
illustrated in Fig.
[2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks"):
(1) Proximity-based unit ordering: We enhance spatial reasoning via a
greedy nearest-neighbor unit ordering, which explicitly encodes spatial
relationships into the observation text. Specifically, starting from the
Command Center, each unit is listed after its nearest neighbor unit.
This heuristic helps agents identify interactable structures
effectively. (2) Unit aggregation: We reduce information overload by
aggregating routine worker units into a single representation,
preserving core workers’ information while removing redundant details.
As validated in Section
[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks"),
these techniques improve agent performance.

Observation and Action Interface. As shown in Fig.
[2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks"),
SC2Arena provides a standardized and extensible text-based interface for
StarCraft II. Observations are formatted as a hierarchical text summary,
categorized into six key types: resource levels, unit states, building
statuses, ongoing activities, visible enemy units/structures, and
technological progress. Actions are defined in a unified JSON format,
enabling agents to specify tasks such as unit production, structure
construction, and tactical maneuvers. Each action includes parameters
like unit IDs, target locations, or specific abilities, allowing precise
in-game control. Appendix
[A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Formulation of SC2Arena’s Observation and Action ‣ Appendix A Implementation of SC2Arena ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks")
provides detailed examples of observations and actions.

Implementation details. At each iteration of the gameplay loop, the
agent processes the textual game state, constructs a prompt, and queries
the LLM for a decision. The environment extracts the valid JSON from the
LLM’s output, parses it into an executable action, and executes it. This
design maintains a clear separation between the agent and the
environment. Appendix
[A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 SC2Arena’s Implementation Details ‣ Appendix A Implementation of SC2Arena ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks")
provides more details.

### 3.3 Evaluation Metrics

SC2Arena supports competitive interactions between agents and various
opponents, including built-in AI, rule-based adversaries, or other
agents. We provide a comprehensive set of metrics to assess both
performance and efficiency across these competitive settings.

Performance metrics: (1) Elo Rating (ELO): A widely adopted metric in
competitive environments for quantifying agents’ relative levels. It is
derived from agent-vs-agent match outcomes and updates after each
contest. (2) Win Rate (WR): Percentage of games won, typically against
built-in AIs. (3) Time Cost of Winning (TCW): Average duration of
winning games, reflecting strategic efficiency. (4) Supply Block Ratio
(SBR): Percentage of game time during which a player cannot produce new
units due to reaching the supply cap. This metric evaluates a player’s
ability to manage resources and sustain continuous military production.
(5) Resource Utilization Ratio (RUR): Average minerals and gas spent per
game timestep, reflecting economic development.

Efficiency metrics: (6) Tokens Per Decision (TPD): Average number of LLM
tokens per decision. (7) Valid Action Ratio (VAR): Percentage of valid
and executable decisions made by the agent. Detailed formulations are
provided in Appendix
[A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 SC2Arena’s Performance Metrics ‣ Appendix A Implementation of SC2Arena ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks").

## 4 StarEvolve

In this section, we propose StarEvolve, a closed-loop, self-improving,
and self-correcting LLM agent framework for StarCraft II. StarEvolve
comprises a high-level strategic Planner, a low-level Executor, and a
Verifier mechanism for self-correction. Crucially, StarEvolve enhances
its performance by generating high-quality gameplay data and fine-tuning
itself, forming an effective self-improvement loop. This closed-loop
design allows smaller LLMs to achieve competitive performance against
challenging opponents.

### 4.1 Hierarchical Self-Correction Framework

Deploying LLM agents for StarCraft II presents challenges, due to the
game’s vast low-level action space and the need for precise unit
selection in JSON syntax, which often results in invalid actions,
distracting agents from high-level strategy ([Tam et al.
2024](#bib.bib16)). To address this, StarEvolve employs a two-tier
architecture: a high-level Planner generates strategic commands, and a
low-level Executor translates them into JSON actions. However, the
Planner may produce commands violating resource constraints or
referencing invalid units, while the Executor can generate syntactically
incorrect or infeasible actions. To mitigate these errors, StarEvolve
integrates Verifiers for both components, enabling iterative
self-correction. The Planner’s Verifier validates strategic commands
against expert rules, while the Executor’s Verifier ensures action
syntax and feasibility. Fig.
[3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 Introduction to SC2Arena ‣ 3 Benchmark: SC2Arena ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks")
depicts this process.

Planner. The Planner generates high-level strategic commands $`c`$ in
natural language, such as “Build a Barracks”, based on the game
observations $`o`$ from SC2Arena. To enhance command quality, the
Planner’s Verifier, also an LLM, evaluates each command. If any rule is
violated, the Verifier offers structured feedback and suggestions
$`f_{\text{p}}`$, allowing the Planner to iteratively refine its output.
This design is highly extensible and supports seamless integration of
additional expert knowledge. Appendix
[B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Planner ‣ Appendix B Implementation of StarEvolve ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks")
provides detailed prompts and rule lists.

Executor. The Executor translates the Planner’s natural language
commands $`c`$ into executable, low-level JSON actions $`a`$. To ensure
the feasibility of actions, the Executor’s Verifier validates each JSON
output by checking (1) JSON syntax correction, (2) parameter and action
validity, and (3) resource feasibility. Invalid actions also trigger
structured feedback $`f_{\text{e}}`$, enabling iterative
self-correction. Appendix
[B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Executor ‣ Appendix B Implementation of StarEvolve ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks")
provides implementation details.

### 4.2 Self-Improvement via Fine-tuning

In this subsection, we design a self-improvement loop based on SFT as in
Fig.
[3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 Introduction to SC2Arena ‣ 3 Benchmark: SC2Arena ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks"),
which enables the agent to extract strategic insights from its own
high-performing behaviors and enhance its performance. We introduce the
self-improvement loop from the following perspectives:

SFT Data Construction. We construct the SFT dataset from winning game
trajectories, where Chain-of-Thought (CoT) naturally emerges through
in-game prompting. To ensure dataset quality, we design a scoring
function inspired by reinforcement learning. Each action $`a_{t}`$ at
timestep $`t`$ is evaluated based on its discounted future impact on
core game metrics, including the converted mineral/vespene values of all
units and structures, as well as the counts of army and mining units.
Formally, the score aggregates temporally discounted gains over a
20-step horizon (30 seconds), where $`M`$ denotes the metric set and
$`V_{m}(o_{t})`$ represents the value of metric $`m`$ on the game
observation $`o_{t}`$:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\text{score}(a_{t})=\sum_{k=1}^{20}\gamma^{k}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}}\left(V_{m}(o_{t+k})-V_{m}(o_{t})\right),~\gamma=0.95
``` |  | (1) |

To ensure comparability, raw metrics are normalized to zero mean and
unit variance. Actions with scores above a predefined threshold are
retained, prioritizing those that optimize both short-term tactical
benefits and long-term strategic impact. Appendix
[A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 SC2Arena’s Performance Metrics ‣ Appendix A Implementation of SC2Arena ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks")
provides the full evaluated metric list and more details.

Fine-tuning Planner and Executor. To enhance performance, we train the
Planner and Executor with verifier-guided rejection sampling.
Specifically, the Planner is trained on $`\langle`$observation
$`o_{t}`$, verified high-level command $`c_{t}`$$`\rangle`$ pairs, while
the Executor is trained on $`\langle`$(observation $`o_{t}`$, high-level
command $`c_{t}`$), verified JSON action $`a_{t}`$$`\rangle`$ pairs.
Crucially, the SFT loss is computed solely on the final output of each
module’s self-correction chain, masking all intermediate refinement
steps. This approach mimics rejection sampling: the Verifier iteratively
discards suboptimal outputs, accepting only the terminal responses as
training targets, thereby learning the optimal decisions.

Fine-tuning Planner’s Verifier. To improve verification efficiency, we
train the Planner’s Verifier using self-correction trajectories. For
each successfully verified high-level command $`c^{+}`$, we construct
training data using the final accepted command and its immediate
rejected predecessor $`c^{-}`$, in the form of $`\langle`$rejected
command $`c^{-}`$ + feedback $`f_{\text{p}}^{-}`$ $`\rightarrow`$
accepted command $`c^{+}`$ + feedback $`f_{\text{p}}^{+}`$ $`\rangle`$.
This method performs implicit contrastive learning, enabling the
Verifier to better capture the boundary between valid and invalid
commands compared to learning from isolated examples, thus enhancing
learning effectiveness.

Implementation details. We collect high-quality gameplay data to
fine-tune the Planner, Executor, and Planner’s Verifier. Specifically,
these data are merged into a single, unified dataset to train an LLM,
enabling it to learn both decision-making and self-correction
strategies. Details on the SFT process are provided in Appendix
[B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Supervised Fine-tuning ‣ Appendix B Implementation of StarEvolve ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks").

## 5 Experiments

In this section, we conduct comprehensive experiments to address three
key research questions: Q1: Can SC2Arena effectively evaluate the
performance of LLM-driven agents in decision-making scenarios? Q2: Does
StarEvolve consistently generate effective and robust strategies while
improving performance through self-improvement mechanisms? Q3: What are
the contributions of each modules in SC2Arena and StarEvolve to overall
performance?

### 5.1 Setup

In this subsection, we outline the experimental setup. For the
agent-vs-agent evaluation, we employ DeepSeek-V3-0324 ([DeepSeek-AI
2024](#bib.bib3)), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ([Team 2024](#bib.bib17)), and
Qwen3-8B ([Team 2025](#bib.bib18)) models with simple, predefined
prompts as baselines, as details in Appendix
[C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Design of Simple Baseline Agents ‣ Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks").
For the agent-vs-built-in AI evaluation, we compete against Harder (LV6)
and VeryHard (LV7) opponents, which represent the highest non-cheating
difficulty levels. These results are compared to prior works ([Ma et al.
2024](#bib.bib9)). Performance is evaluated using metrics defined in
Section
[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Evaluation Metrics ‣ 3 Benchmark: SC2Arena ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks").
Specifically, Elo ratings are initialized at 1000 for all agents and
updated using a K-factor of 32 based on match outcomes. Appendix
[C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Experimental Setup ‣ Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks")
provides further details.

### 5.2 Main Results

Agent-vs-Agent. To evaluate the performance of StarEvolve against
baseline agents, we conduct pairwise matches across 5 games each of
Terran vs. Terran (TvT), Zerg vs. Zerg (ZvZ), and Protoss vs. Protoss
(PvP), using the outcomes to calculate Elo ratings. As shown in Fig.
[4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4 StarEvolve ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks"),
StarEvolve (SFT) achieves the highest Elo rating of 1211 for Terran,
outperforming DeepSeek. For Protoss and Zerg, StarEvolve (SFT) also
achieves competitive ratings of 1080 and 1096. These results highlight
three key insights: ① SC2Arena effectively supports Elo-based agent
ranking; ② StarEvolve demonstrates strong performance, outperforming
most baselines; and ③ fine-tuning significantly enhances performance,
enabling StarEvolve to match or surpass DeepSeek in specific scenarios.

Agent-vs-Built-In AI. Furthermore, we evaluated the performance of
StarEvolve without SFT using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B (no_think),
DeepSeek-V3-0324, and fine-tuned StarEvolve with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct,
following the fine-tuning process in Section
[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Self-Improvement via Fine-tuning ‣ 4 StarEvolve ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks").
We use metrics in Section
[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Evaluation Metrics ‣ 3 Benchmark: SC2Arena ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks"),
excluding Elo, for evaluation. As shown in Table
[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4 StarEvolve ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks"),
StarEvolve consistently outperforms challenging built-in AIs across
diverse LLMs, demonstrating its robustness. Fine-tuning further improves
performance: for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, fine-tuning increases the win rate
from 55% to 71% at LV6 and reduces token consumption from 2298 to 1451.
At the more challenging LV7, the fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model
achieves a 73% win rate, approaching DeepSeek’s performance. These
findings demonstrate that StarEvolve is effective across models and
scenarios, with significant improvements after fine-tuning.

Comparison with prior work. We compare our method with [Ma et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib9) in the Protoss vs. Zerg setting, the primary focus of
their study, using 20 matches. As shown in Table
[5](#S5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 5.1 Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks"),
despite leveraging stronger GPT-based LLMs, [Ma et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib9) achieves lower win rates than our approach. Notably,
[Ma et al. (2024)](#bib.bib9) simplifies the problem: their agent
generates only high-level decisions, while low-level actions are
executed via predefined scripts, thereby reducing game complexity. In
contrast, our method outperforms this baseline with a smaller model
while addressing the more challenging full low-level action space.

### 5.3 Ablation Study

SC2Arena’s optimized observation. To evaluate the impact of our
observation optimization techniques, we conducted ablation experiments
by removing two key components: unit ordering and aggregation. We
performed 20 TvT, ZvZ, and PvP matches for each configuration and
analyzed the results. As shown in Table
[8](#A5.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix E Additional Experimental Results ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks")
in Appendix
[E](#A5 "Appendix E Additional Experimental Results ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks"),
removing these techniques significantly degrades performance.
Specifically, removing unit ordering impairs spatial relationship
modeling or aggregation, reducing the Valid Action Ratio (VAR). This
suggests the critical role of both techniques in enabling efficient
decision-making within StarCraft II’s complex environment.

Self-correction mechanism and the Planner. We ablated the Verifier and
Planner modules to assess their contributions by conducting 20 TvT, ZvZ,
and PvP matches for each configuration. As shown in Table
[3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.1 Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks"),
disabling the Verifier module reduced the win rate by 18% and VAR by
30%. Removing the Planner module led to a 15% win rate in all matches.
This shows the essential role of hierarchical self-correction and
strategic planning in robust decision-making.

Scoring function for SFT data collection. To evaluate the effectiveness
of the scoring function, we trained on all winning matches instead of
using the function to filter experimental data. We conducted 20 TvT
matches and analyzed the results. As shown in Table
[4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.1 Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks"),
removing the scoring function significantly decreases performance, with
win rates dropping from 73% to 41% and VAR decreasing by 33%. These
results highlight that, even when distilling high-quality data from
high-performance models like DeepSeek, selecting the best data remains
essential. Our scoring function effectively identifies key game
indicators, ensuring better data selection.

### 5.4 Visualizations of Gameplay

In this subsection, we demonstrate StarEvolve’s strategic planning and

and secures victory with a decisive offensive (Fig.

This illustrates StarEvolve’s capacity to adapt and strategize

## 6 Conclusion

In this paper, we introduce SC2Arena, a comprehensive StarCraft II
benchmark for evaluating LLMs agents in decision-making tasks. SC2Arena
supports full-length game contexts, diverse race configurations,
low-level action spaces, and agent-vs-agent gameplay, enabling robust
performance assessment and ranking. We also present StarEvolve, a
closed-loop agent framework that combines hierarchical planning with
iterative self-correction and continuous self-improvement through
supervised fine-tuning. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of
SC2Arena for agent evaluation and highlight StarEvolve’s ability to
achieve strong performance, including enabling smaller models to compete
effectively against challenging opponents. These results show the
potential of SC2Arena and StarEvolve to advance research in complex
decision-making for LLMs.

## Appendix A Implementation of SC2Arena

### A.1 Introduction to StarCraft II

In this subsection, we provide a concise overview of StarCraft II, a
landmark real-time strategy (RTS) game developed by Blizzard
Entertainment. Renowned for its strategic complexity, tactical depth,
and asymmetrical balance between three distinct races, StarCraft II has
become a benchmark for AI research in dynamic, partially observable
environments requiring real-time decision-making.

#### Basic Interface.

The game features a top-down view of the battlefield, with a primary map
display, a minimap for global awareness, and mouse-and-keyboard
controls. Players use the mouse to select units, issue commands, and
navigate the map, while the keyboard enables rapid actions through
hotkeys, such as unit production and camera movement. The minimap allows
monitoring of multiple locations simultaneously, facilitating quick
responses. Resources, including minerals and vespene gas, are displayed
alongside a command panel that provides access to unit and building
functions.

#### Game Objectives and Core Gameplay.

The objective is to defeat opponents by destroying their bases while
protecting one’s own. Success requires a combination of strategic
planning and tactical execution:

- •
  Strategy: Players manage resource collection, base expansion, and
  technological progression to unlock advanced units and upgrades.
  Securing additional resource nodes is essential for sustained
  production, while efficient resource allocation ensures
  competitiveness over time.
- •
  Tactics: Combat relies on precise unit control, such as positioning,
  micro-management (e.g., dodging attacks or optimizing unit abilities),
  and multi-tasking across multiple fronts. The fog of war, which
  obscures unscouted areas, adds to the challenge by limiting available
  information, requiring adaptive decision-making under time
  constraints.

#### Race Mechanisms.

The game’s three asymmetric races—Terran, Zerg, and Protoss—offer
distinct playstyles while maintaining competitive balance:

- •
  Terran: A versatile, mechanically focused race with strong defensive
  capabilities. Terran units and buildings can be repaired, and
  structures like bunkers and siege tanks excel at controlling key
  areas. Add-ons and mobile buildings enhance adaptability, enabling
  positional advantages.
- •
  Zerg: An aggressive, swarm-based race that emphasizes rapid production
  and map control. Units are spawned from larvae at hatcheries,
  requiring efficient resource management and expansion. Zerg structures
  must be built on creep, an organic terrain that spreads dynamically,
  encouraging offensive gameplay.
- •
  Protoss: A technologically advanced race featuring powerful but costly
  units. Protoss structures require energy supplied by pylons, and units
  are warped in rather than produced conventionally. Shields that
  regenerate over time promote hit-and-run tactics, while warp gates
  allow rapid reinforcement, favoring decisive engagements.

The combination of economic strategy, technological progression, and
tactical combat, along with the unique characteristics of each race,
creates a highly dynamic and competitive environment. StarCraft II
epitomizes the challenges of real-time multi-agent systems, making it an
enduring platform for AI research.

### A.2 Formulation of SC2Arena’s Observation and Action

SC2Arena provides a standardized text-based interface designed for LLM
agents. Observations are presented as hierarchical textual summaries of
the game state, employing two key optimizations to minimize cognitive
load while retaining essential information:

- •
  Unit aggregation, which groups units performing similar tasks (e.g.,
  mining SCVs), and
- •
  Proximity-based unit ordering, inspired by the Traveling Salesman
  Problem (TSP), which sequences units and buildings based on spatial
  proximity, starting from the Command Center. This structure forms an
  explicit topological map, aiding LLMs in understanding functional
  dependencies (e.g., Barracks-TechLab) and battlefield positions
  without processing raw game data. Actions are encoded in a unified
  JSON format, allowing for precise multi-unit commands.

#### Observation Example.

The textualized observation encompasses the following information:
current game settings (time, race, map), resource status (minerals,
vespene, supply), the state of allied units, abilities of allied
units/buildings, the status of visible enemy units/buildings,
descriptions of allied abilities, history of allied actions, and the map
resources distribution. To facilitate model decisions with supplementary
information, SC2Arena incorporates brief descriptions of the tech tree
and available actions specific. An example is provided as follows:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### Action Example.

In SC2Arena, executable actions are represented as a list of JSON
objects. Every action object requires two primary keys: action,
specifying the command, and units, indicating the unit(s) involved. For
specific actions, additional keys such as target_unit or target_position
are needed to specify the target entity or location. An example is
provided asffollows:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### A.3 SC2Arena’s Implementation Details

#### How SC2Arena Interacts with StarCraft II.

SC2Arena is built on the widely used Python-sc2 library, which provides
a Python API for interacting with the StarCraft II game client via its
raw API. We extended this library to create a standardized environment
for LLM-based agents by enabling real-time conversion of complex game
states into structured text observations, and translating the LLM’s
JSON-formatted actions into executable game commands.

#### Computational Resources Required.

Running experiments in SC2Arena involves two key components: the agent
(LLM) and the environment (game client). Agent (LLM Server): Our
experiments used a server with an AMD EPYC 64-Core CPU, 503GB RAM, and
six NVIDIA A100 (80GB) GPUs, running Ubuntu 18.04, Python 3.9+, and
necessary deep learning frameworks. Detailed environmental requirements
are provided in our anonymous code repository. Environment (Game
Client): The StarCraft II game client can run on a standard desktop or
laptop computer. A local installation of StarCraft II on a compatible
operating system (Windows or macOS) is required.

### A.4 SC2Arena’s Performance Metrics

In this subsection, we describe the evaluation metrics used for
SC2Arena. First, we explain the calculation of the Elo rating. Then, we
introduce the other metrics and provide their formulation.

#### Elo Rating System.

We employ the standard Elo rating system to quantify agent performance
in agent-vs-agent comparisons. Each agent starts with an initial rating
of $`R_{0}=1000`$. After a match between agent $`A`$ (rating $`R_{A}`$)
and agent $`B`$ (rating $`R_{B}`$), their ratings update as:

1.  1.
    Expected Score Calculation: $`A`$’s expected score is derived from
    the rating difference:

    |     |                                          |     |
    |-----|------------------------------------------|-----|
    |     |
           ``` math
           E_{A}=\frac{1}{1+10^{(R_{B}-R_{A})/400}}
           ```                                       |     |

    $`B`$’s expected score is $`E_{B}=1-E_{A}`$.
2.  2.
    Actual Score Assignment: The outcome $`S_{A}`$ is assigned as:

    |  |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|----|
    |  | $`\displaystyle S_{A}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\begin{cases}1.0&\text{win}\\
    0.5&\text{tie}\\
    0.0&\text{loss}\end{cases},`$ |  |
    |  | $`\displaystyle S_{B}`$ | $`\displaystyle=1-S_{A}.`$ |  |
3.  3.
    Rating Update: New ratings are calculated using:

    |  |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|----|
    |  | $`\displaystyle R^{\prime}_{A}`$ | $`\displaystyle=R_{A}+K\cdot(S_{A}-E_{A}),`$ |  |
    |  | $`\displaystyle R^{\prime}_{B}`$ | $`\displaystyle=R_{B}+K\cdot(S_{B}-E_{B}),`$ |  |

    where $`K=32`$ is the update sensitivity factor.

Matches are processed in random order. Ratings update sequentially after
each match, with new agents initialized to $`R_{0}`$ upon first
appearance. Final rankings are determined by descending order of
converged ratings.

#### Other metrics.

Then, we introduce the other metrics and provide their formulation.

1.  1.
    Win Rate (WR): The proportion of games won against a fixed set of
    opponents (e.g., built-in AIs). It reflects overall effectiveness in
    achieving victory under standardized conditions.

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \mathrm{WR}=\frac{\text{Number of Wins}}{\text{Total Games Played}}\times 100\%
    ``` |  |
2.  2.
    Time Cost of Winning (TCW): Average duration of victorious games,
    measured in game seconds. It indicates strategic efficiency; lower
    TCW implies faster execution of winning strategies.

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \mathrm{TCW}=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{wins}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{wins}}}T_{i}
    ``` |  |

    where $`T_{i}`$ is the duration of the $`i`$-th winning game.
3.  3.
    Supply Block Ratio (SBR): Fraction of game time during which unit
    production is halted due to insufficient supply capacity. It
    evaluates macro-management skill; lower SBR denotes optimal resource
    allocation and production continuity.

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \mathrm{SBR}=\frac{\text{Time Supply Capped}}{\text{Total Game Time}}\times 100\%
    ``` |  |
4.  4.
    Resource Utilization Ratio (RUR): Average resources (minerals + gas)
    spent per game timestep. It quantifies economic efficiency; higher
    RUR indicates effective resource conversion into units/upgrades.

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \mathrm{RUR}=\frac{\text{Total Resources Spent}}{\text{Total Game Timesteps}}
    ``` |  |
5.  5.
    Tokens Per Decision (TPD): Average output token count consumed by
    the LLM to generate a single in-game decision. It measures
    computational efficiency of the LLM agent; lower TPD implies leaner
    prompt engineering and faster inference.

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \mathrm{TPD}=\frac{\text{Total Tokens Processed}}{\text{Total Decisions Made}}
    ``` |  |
6.  6.
    Valid Action Ratio (VAR): Proportion of agent decisions that are
    syntactically and semantically executable in the game environment.
    It assesses action robustness; higher VAR indicates better alignment
    with game rules and context awareness.

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \mathrm{VAR}=\frac{\text{Valid Decisions}}{\text{Total Decisions Attempted}}\times 100\%
    ``` |  |

## Appendix B Implementation of StarEvolve

### B.1 Planner

The StarEvolve Planner analyzes the current game state and generates
natural language command directives using a structured prompt template.
In this template, obs_text represents the textualized game state,
rules_list is a dynamic list of expert knowledge, and plan_example
consists of plan examples for different races.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Below is a complete prompt example from a Protoss vs. Protoss match.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

We provide an example output of the Planner from DeepSeek-V3-0324 as
follows. It employs a step-by-step reasoning process and outputs five
plans in JSON format.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### B.2 Planner Verifier

The Planner’s Verifier in StarEvolve validates the plans generated by
the Planner and identifies errors using a set of dynamic expert
knowledge. This process employs the prompt template as follows, where
given_command refers to the plans produced by the Planner, and
rules_list is the same as the part of the Planner prompt.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The Verifier operates using a dynamic knowledge list comprising expert
rules specific to three races. This list includes a small, static set
that is always active and a larger, conditional set triggered by
specific in-game events. For instance, the first three shared knowledge
entries are permanently included in decision-making, while the 12th
Terran entry is added only when supply is low. The full knowledge bases
for each race are detailed below.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

We provide the output of DeepSeek-V3-0324 Verifier, which evaluated the
plan generated in Section
[B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Planner ‣ Appendix B Implementation of StarEvolve ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks").
The Planner uses the final error message for reflection and correction
to produce a revised plan. We set a maximum of 3 rounds for the Verifier
to be invoked in a single decision-making process. The Planner’s final
output is determined either by successful validation or by reaching the
maximum number of attempts.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### B.3 Executor

The StarEvolve Executor executes the Planner’s plan based on the current
game state, producing a valid JSON action as required by SC2Arena. For
example, given the command “Train a Marine”, the Executor should
identify an idle Barracks and generate the corresponding
BARRACKSTRAIN_MARINE action with the appropriate unit ID.

Below is the prompt template for the StarEvolve Executor, where
plan_text is the final output version of Planner.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

We provide an example output of Executor by DeepSeek-V3-0324 as follows.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Unlike the Planner, the Executor’s Verifier is implemented as a Python
function. It validates the JSON list generated by the Executor by
checking syntax, resource constraints, action feasibility, and target
existence. This process enables the agent to identify errors before
executing actions in the game. For instance, in the provided Executor
output example, the Verifier flagged errors related to insufficient
resources. The maximum number of verification attempts is limited to 3.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### B.4 Supervised Fine-tuning

The supervised fine-tuning data selection process uses a scoring
function controlled by two hyperparameters: the forward step size
($`K`$) and the discount factor ($`\gamma`$). Specifically, $`K`$ is set
to 20, corresponding to a temporal window of approximately 30 seconds,
chosen to capture the immediate effects of actions, while minimizing the
influence of longer-term confounding factors. The discount factor
$`\gamma`$ is adjusted such that the cumulative discount over this
window is approximately 0.36, i.e., $`\gamma^{20}\approx 0.36`$. Scores
are then Z-score normalized independently for each 30-second interval,
and data points with standardized scores greater than 0.1 are selected
for fine-tuning.

For the fine-tuning process, we employed a full-parameter approach. The
detailed settings are as follows:

- •
  Fine-tuning Method: Full-parameter fine-tuning
- •
  Training Framework: LLaMA-Factory
- •
  Distributed Training: DeepSpeed ZeRO-3
- •
  Epochs: 2
- •
  Batch Size: 32
- •
  Learning Rate: 5e-5 with a cosine decay schedule
- •
  Warm-up Ratio: 0.1

Table

presents a detailed breakdown of the SFT dataset, organized by race and
the target agent component.

### B.5 Implementation Details

The decision-making timing in StarEvolve is controlled by a two-tiered
temporal trigger. The primary trigger activates whenever the agent’s
mineral supply exceeds 170, with decisions made at fixed intervals of 10
game iterations (approximately 1.5 seconds). To ensure responsiveness, a
secondary failsafe trigger guarantees that a decision is made at least
once every 100 iterations, regardless of the primary trigger’s
activation. After each execution of the failsafe trigger, it is
rescheduled for 100 iterations later.

In StarCraft II, workers constitute a significant portion of
controllable units. Delegating their tedious resource-gathering tasks to
an LLM agent would hinder its decision-making capabilities. To address
this, StarEvolve employs a rule-based approach that periodically assigns
workers to the nearest resource nodes based on the current levels of
Minerals and Vespene Gas. Additionally, units are programmed to
automatically attack, prioritizing enemies with the lowest health.

## Appendix C Experimental Details

### C.1 Experimental Setup

The experiments were conducted on the following platform:

- •
  CPU: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8457C
- •
  GPU: 8 $`\times`$ NVIDIA H20 (96GB)
- •
  Operating System: Debian GNU/Linux 10 (buster)
- •
  Python: 3.12.11
- •
  PyTorch: 2.7.0+cu128

Specifically, all experiments were conducted on the Flat48 map from the
“Melee” map pack, which can be obtained from the official s2client-proto
repository. In agent-vs-built-in AI experiments, the agent competed
against Harder (LV6) and VeryHard (LV7) difficulty levels, which are the
highest non-cheating difficulties. The built-in AI employed a “random
build” style, utilizing a diverse range of randomized build orders and
strategies. This ensures the opponent is varied and challenging, rather
than a predictable, fixed adversary.

The deployment and API calls for different models were handled as
described below:

- •
  Qwen Series Models: Deployed using vLLM (version 0.9.2). For Qwen3-8B,
  a hybrid reasoning model, we employ it in its non-reasoning mode
  (activated by adding /no_think to prompts) to avoid the excessive
  latency of its reasoning process.
- •
  DeepSeek Models: Accessed via the official DeepSeek API.

strategy, we present two representative cases of matches between

Unlike agents focused primarily on micro-level unit control, our model
demonstrates robust macro-level strategic decision-making, reflecting
human-like strategic thinking and tactical foresight. Fig.
[6](#A4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix D Visualization Results ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks")
highlights this capability across entire matches.

#### Case 1: Terran Agent (Fine-tuned) - Proactive Offensive Strategy.

In this scenario, the fine-tuned Terran agent executes a proactive,
overwhelming offensive strategy.

- •
  Early Game - Fig.
  [6](#A4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix D Visualization Results ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks")(a):
  The agent follows standard economic build orders, balancing resource
  expansion (e.g., SCV production, base construction) with technology
  upgrades. Early Barracks construction ensures defensive capabilities
  while supporting continuous Marine production, establishing a strong
  foundation for mid-game transitions.
- •
  Mid Game - Fig.
  [6](#A4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix D Visualization Results ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks")(b):
  Leveraging an economic advantage, the agent maximizes unit production
  by building additional Barracks and Factories to avoid resource
  saturation. A decisive ‘ATTACK’ command is issued after amassing
  sufficient forces, demonstrating a deliberate focus on offensive
  strategy rather than passive defense.
- •
  Late Game - Fig.
  [6](#A4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix D Visualization Results ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks")(c):
  The agent achieves victory by systematically destroying the enemy’s
  main base and eliminating remaining forces. Key Insight: The final
  engagement showcases deliberate tactical positioning, as the agent’s
  forces form a concave formation around the opponent’s base, maximizing
  crossfire efficiency and cutting off escape routes. This sequence
  demonstrates the agent’s coherent strategy from economic preparation
  to decisive combat.

#### Case 2: Zerg Agent (without SFT) - Adaptive Defense and Map Control.

In this case, the baseline Zerg agent demonstrates adaptive defensive
strategies and effective map control.

- •
  Early Game - Fig.
  [6](#A4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix D Visualization Results ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks")(d):
  The agent displays adaptability by converting Overlords to increase
  supply and enable scouting. Tactical Response: When harassed by enemy
  Zerglings, only a small subset of Drones is committed to defense while
  the majority continue mining, balancing economic growth with defense.
- •
  Mid Game - Fig.
  [6](#A4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix D Visualization Results ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks")(e):
  Facing a large enemy assault, the agent employs a defensive strategy
  by leveraging Zerg-specific mechanics. Key Maneuver: Expanding Creep
  coverage via Creep Tumors provides vision and enhances unit mobility
  within controlled areas. These actions blunt the enemy’s offensive and
  create favorable conditions for a counter-attack.
- •
  Late Game - Fig.
  [6](#A4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix D Visualization Results ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks")(f):
  After repelling the attack, the agent gains the initiative. Strategic
  Advantage: By aggressively expanding Creep coverage and mass-producing
  Zerglings, the agent achieves superior vision and mobility across the
  map. This positional and informational dominance allows the agent to
  concentrate forces for a decisive offensive, ultimately overwhelming
  the opponent’s depleted resources and constrained positioning.

#### Case 3: Protoss Agent (without SFT) - Adaptive Attack Based on Reconnaissance.

- •

#### Ablation on SC2Arena’s optimized observation.

To evaluate the impact of our observation optimization techniques, we
conducted ablation experiments by removing two key components: unit
ordering and aggregation. We performed 20 TvT, ZvZ, and PvP matches for
each configuration and analyzed the results. As shown in Table
[8](#A5.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix E Additional Experimental Results ‣ SC2Arena and StarEvolve: Benchmark and Self-Improvement Framework for LLMs in Complex Decision-Making Tasks"),
removing these techniques significantly degrades performance.
Specifically, removing unit ordering impairs spatial relationship
modeling or aggregation, reducing the Valid Action Ratio (VAR). This
suggests the critical role of both techniques in enabling efficient
decision-making within StarCraft II’s complex environment.
````
